text: this. No protection. No guidance. No particular value to anything that might be watching. Just a man in a flooding hallway. Just more meat in the tank. The current pulled him under again, and this time when he fought back to the surface it was pure reflex, nothing behind it but the dumb animal insistence on one more breath. That was all he had left. Ch 8 – Flotsam The hallway screamed with water and metal. Orela’s flashlight arced wildly through the chaos, cutting sharp glints into the shattered mess around them — a locker door hanging open, water sheeting off the ceiling in solid curtains, the shape of Jake braced in a corner with Dwight pinned against him, David trying to hide his face against his arms in a futile effort to keep the back spray out of his sinuses. And still the current surged — not enough to sweep them fully, but more than enough to throw them off balance. She swept right. Debris. She swept left. Wall. She swept further and the beam caught something that wasn't wall and wasn't debris — a shape, flailing, bouncing off the lockers like a ragdoll. She didn't place him immediately — the distance was wrong, the shape was wrong without the robes reading the way they usually did — and then Leon's hand closed on her arm and she felt him go rigid beside her, and that was enough. She followed his eyes, looked again, and this time the shape resolved. She grabbed Leon's sleeve and pointed, hard, then turned and started waving at the others. Dwight saw where they were looking and moved without thinking. The water sloshed hard as he pushed off the wall, slamming forward through the current. One moment he was against the wall with Jake's arm across him, the next he was pushing forward through the water, shouldering past without explanation, eyes fixed on the shape tumbling down the hallway. He didn't think about the current. Didn't think about the water level or the pressure waves or the fact that his legs had barely been reliable for the last hour. He just moved — some part of him that operated below the threshold of good judgment simply seeing someone struggling and moving in to help. David's hand caught his arm and yanked him back hard enough to stagger him, pulling him close enough to make himself heard over the roar. “DON’T! What the hell do you think you’re doing?!” "We can't just leave him!" He pulled against David's grip, a fierce determination in his eyes. “We sure as fuck CAN!” “David—” “Did you forget what he IS?” Jake grimaced behind them, catching the light as it rocked in Orela’s hand. She didn’t join the argument — didn’t seem to hear it at all, really — as she pressed the flashlight into Jake’s hands, pulling his arm up to angle the beam down the hall with the clear intent for him to keep her way lit up. She motioned to Leon to follow her, before bracing her arms and beginning to push through the deepening flood. She had been unable to feel helpful at all this entire time, with David clearly needing help but rejecting it, and the others barely standing still long enough for her to even assess them. But here was something she COULD accomplish. Killer or not, she wasn’t going to just let someone drown not even 60 feet away. Not if she could do something about it. Behind her, Dwight met David's eyes. It wasn't a long standoff. Dwight didn't have David's build or his stubbornness, and they both knew it — a straight contest of wills between them had a predictable outcome. But Dwight held the look, steady, and something in it must have landed, because David's grip on his arm loosened by degrees. Dwight wrenched his arm back, and David finally let go. He watched Dwight half swim, half sprint off after Orela, then turned back to resume battering at the door. Someone had to keep working on the exit. Someone had to be practical about this. He put his shoulder into it again and tried not to think about what was happening down the hall. He needed to get the others out before their own altruism got them all killed. Leon made it two steps. His breath hitched as he watched Orela go. His feet planted, shoulders tense, the flicker of the beam reflecting off her soaked shirt as she moved into the darkness, Dwight hot on her heels. Leon moved to follow the rescue team but froze in place. His brain screamed at him to move — go — but the water was so high now, pulling at his legs and stomach in unnatural swirls of current. The surface was so intensely dark. The faint memory of a black claw coiled towards him, seizing his spine. He tried to step forward and nothing moved. Every inch of him had locked up, heart hammering, legs unwilling. Jake’s touch on his arm shattered the moment and he startled, eyes wild and chest heaving, as the flashlight was pushed into his hands. “I got you, man. Just keep us lit as best you can, ok? I’ll make sure they come back.” Leon swallowed once, eyes flicking to Orela’s shrinking silhouette, then back to Jake. An embarrassed nod of understanding passed between them and Jake turned to paddle after the others, leaving Leon to curse at his own freeze up. The moment had passed but the sting of it sat deep in him as he trained the light down the hall onto his friends. Orela’s boots skidded once, then bit. She leaned hard into the current, arms braced forward. Danny breached the surface in a sputtering mess of limbs and panic just as she reached him, and she snagged him — fingers locking in the collar of his sodden robes. The drag was considerable.
